Where the Timescale ingest path spends its time — plain INSERT, non-unique (ref_id, ts) index

acquirium ums-timescale-fix @ d6b6e1a5f20b — the CSV → polars → melt → Arrow → Timescale pipeline replayed stage by stage outside the server, on the cloud VM (4 vCPU / 16 GiB), timescale/timescaledb (PG 17.11, TimescaleDB 2.29.2). Same functions, same SQL, same order, same data (2026-09-10T17:43 UTC).

Findings

  • Dropping ON CONFLICT and the unique constraint doubles ingest. All 1000 files (682.6M rows) merged in 36.2 min at 314k rows/s. On the 670 files the baseline managed in its 50-minute cap, this variant took 25.1 min against 50.0 min: 2.0× end to end. The acquirium end-to-end run of this branch took 77.4 min for the same 1000 files.
  • The merge statement itself is 3.1× cheaper: 1.79 µs/row against 5.49 µs/row on the same 452M rows. EXPLAIN on the same file (737k rows) shows why: 4.0 shared-buffer hits per row instead of 8.0, and 2 WAL records per row instead of 3. The ON CONFLICT arbiter probe (a full b-tree descent on the unique index before every insert, plus the speculative-insertion token in WAL) was half the work of the Insert node. The remaining cost is the heap insert plus one b-tree insert into the non-unique index, still on CPU in a single backend (91% of samples on CPU; WAL-write waits appeared at 4% now that the backend generates WAL faster than the wal writer drains it).
  • The merge is no longer alone at the top. Of the 36.2 min: merge 54%, COPY into the staging table 24%, everything Python-side 17%. The Sort feeding the insert (external merge on disk, work_mem 16 MB) is now 29% of the statement (0.32 s of 1.12 s on the 737k-row file), so work_mem and the staging COPY are the next things worth looking at, not the Python code.
  • Cost stays flat with table size (1.60 µs/row over the first 100 files, 1.63 over the last 100, 36 GB heap + 22 GB index at the end, 101 chunks). The two plateaus at ~4 µs/row in the chart (83 files, around files 207–300 and 940–968) are host noise, not the index: during those files the CSV read, the melt and the COPY slowed by the same 2.5–3× while the backend stayed on CPU and the container's CPU share did not change, which is the VM getting fewer cycles from the shared host. Outside them the merge runs at 1.43 µs/row, 3.8× the baseline; the 2.0× end-to-end figure includes that noise, so it is a conservative number. The index is the same size as the unique one; uniqueness costs nothing on disk, only per-row CPU on the write.
  • Correctness caveat: the constraint was doing work. The variant stored 682,580,597 rows; acquirium and the unique-index run stored 682,522,976 for the same files. The 57,621 extra rows (0.008%) are (ref_id, ts) pairs that occur in more than one CSV: consecutive DPR exports overlap by a few minutes. The Python dedupe in _prepare_frame only removes duplicates within one batch; cross-file duplicates were absorbed by ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and are now stored twice. Any read that assumes one row per (stream, ts) would see them. Keeping the write path this fast while still enforcing uniqueness means deduplicating against the table cheaply, for example an anti-join on the batch's time range before the insert, or accepting duplicates and deduplicating on read.
  • WAL and checkpoints: 99 GB of WAL (158 B/row), 193 requested checkpoints in 36 min with max_wal_size = 1 GB; the checkpointer wrote continuously. Same side cost as the baseline, now proportionally bigger because the merge got cheaper.

Baseline vs this variant

Baseline = yesterday's run of the branch as is (INSERT … ON CONFLICT (ref_id, ts) DO UPDATE against the unique index), 670 files in 50.0 min. This run = plain INSERT, non-unique (ref_id, ts) index, 1000 files in 36.2 min. Same VM, same container image and tuning, same data in the same order, same Python path (the dedupe in _prepare_frame still runs, so the same rows are written). Per-row numbers below are over the first 670 files, which both runs processed (452 M rows).

Merge SQL used in this run:

INSERT INTO timeseries (ref_id, ts, numeric_value, text_value)
                SELECT r.ref_id, i.ts, i.numeric_value, i.text_value
                FROM _acquirium_incoming_timeseries AS i
                JOIN ref_ids AS r USING (ref_uri)
                ORDER BY r.ref_id, i.ts

Index DDL applied after ensure_table: DROP INDEX idx_timeseries_ref_ts_unique; CREATE INDEX idx_timeseries_ref_ts ON timeseries (ref_id, ts). Indexes on timeseries: CREATE INDEX idx_timeseries_ref_ts ON public.timeseries USING btree (ref_id, ts).

The Sort + Hash Join feeding the insert finish in well under a second; the rest of the statement is the Insert on timeseries node itself: for every row a b-tree descent on idx_timeseries_ref_ts_unique for the ON CONFLICT arbiter check, the heap insert, the index insert, and the WAL records for both.

5. Method and provenance

  • Code under test: public github.com/DataDrivenCPS/acquirium branch ums-timescale-fix, head d6b6e1a5f20b (remote) == d6b6e1a5f20b (clone). The tracer imports to_observations, IngestDriver.normalize_observations, assign_stream_value_kind, compute_ref_uri, TimescaleStore (schema via ensure_table, ensure_stream_refs, stream_value_kind, _prepare_frame) from that clone and reproduces the client/route/manager glue inline. The five SQL statements of _insert_frame are copied verbatim and checked against the source at start-up: store.drop, store.create_temp, store.copy, store.ref_ids, store.merge, store.write_csv, store.dedupe, manager.value_kind_per_stream, manager.replace_maps, app.from_arrow_partition, client.ipc_stream, driver.register_group_by — all 12 checks passed.
  • Not reproduced: the HTTP hop (loopback POST of the Arrow body), the RDF graph write on stream registration, FastAPI overhead. Every other step runs the same library call on the same frame.
  • Database: fresh container, timescale/timescaledb@sha256:bc8527e62f70f0766b29515077965025872fabb5349db421565f69ee273baf2d, TS_TUNE_MEMORY=8GB TS_TUNE_NUM_CPUS=4, plus pg_stat_statements and track_io_timing=on (the only differences from the benchmark container). 0 public tables before the schema was created.
  • Instrumentation: perf_counter around each stage; pg_stat_activity sampled at 5 Hz; cgroup CPU every 5 s; EXPLAIN ANALYZE replaces the plain merge on every 25th file (that file's merge time includes instrumentation overhead); py-spy 50 Hz windows (CPU-only native 10 min from t+45 s, then wall/idle 10 min, then raw stacks 25 min). No kernel perf is available in this VM, so the Postgres side is profiled with wait events, EXPLAIN and pg_stat_* rather than a flamegraph.
  • Data: 1000 of the 1000 DPR trailer CSVs (NUL-sanitised set from the 1000-file benchmark), ingest order = sorted path, as the driver does. complete.
  • Versions: polars 1.44.1, pyarrow 25.0.1, psycopg 3.3.5, python 3.12.3.
